newsitem.title: UK: Strong UK sales suggest Xmas surge, early rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Strong UK sales suggest Xmas surge, early rate rise.

text.p: Robust UK retail sales figures for November point to a bumper Christmas for British retailers, analysts said on Thursday.

A 0.7 percent rise in high street sales last month, well above forecast, leaves Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke with an uphill battle to keep interest rates on hold in the coming months. "This fleshes out the picture of continued strength and the ever-present need to raise interest rates to cool the economy," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International.
Economists had expected a 0.5 percent rise in sales after surveys from the Confederation of British Industry and British Retail Consortium had portrayed a more reticent UK consumer.

As it turned out, sales shot up by 3.9 percent year-on-year, well above the 3.4 forecast. "The retail sales confirm that the surveys under-estimated the strength of sales in November. The underlying trend looks strong throughout," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale.
More crucially for the financial markets, ever-wary of possible inflation signals, sales showed no signs of slowing in areas where prices are rising.
Textile, clothing and footwear sales leapt by 2.0 percent in November in spite of prices in the same sector having risen by one percent over the same month.
Household goods prices rose by 1.0 percent last month, retail price data out last week showed, but in this sector too sales rose again, by 0.4 percent.

"There is no negative response to the higher prices we have been seeing. Demand is strengthening and is going to continue to do so in the new year, keeping the pressure on for higher base rates," Rayner said. He forecast a monetary tightening in January or February.
Clarke meets Bank of England Governor Eddie George for their next monetary meeting on January 15. Base rates were last raised on October 30, to six percent.
Any hopes Clarke had of keeping interest rates on hold until elections due by May appear to be disappearing over the horizon.

"The latest rise in November is bound to increase fears of margin-building as high street activity quickens," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. But he was less concerned about the inflationary implications. The three-month rate of growth in sales has slowed sharply since the summer, he said, suggesting retailers can still not hike prices regardless.

Sales were 0.8 percent higher in the three months to November. Back in August, the three-month rate of increase was double that. Nonetheless, Loynes said the data meant George was certain to push for a new year rate rise.

Some economists still expect consumer spending to simmer down in the new year. But with a one penny income tax feeding into pay packets from April and a massive 17.0 billion stg in windfalls from building societies hitting consumers' pockets in the summer, Hannah saw no sign of a downturn.
"You're looking at approximately four percent real growth in sales already and there's a whole load of windfalls to come."
Hannah said an inevitable consequence of falling unemployment was that perceptions of greater job security take root. That in turn will boost high street spending.

If latest jobless figures are credible, Britain's workers should be feeling unusually safe. Data released alongside the sales figures, showed a staggering 95,800 fall in the number of jobless in Britain in November, the largest drop on record.

The total number of unemployed is now below two million for the first time since 1991. "When unemployment is falling rapidly and confidence about future employment and income is increasing, retailers are bound to reap the benefits," Hannah said.
